entries.name: App Store Connect CLI (asc)
entries.use_for: Automate TestFlight, builds, submissions, signing and metadata for Apple apps from scripts or CI.
entries.why: A single Go binary for the App Store Connect API, with a matching pack of 25 agent skills.
entries.summary: A fast, scriptable CLI for the App Store Connect API. It automates release work for iOS, macOS, tvOS and visionOS, from review status checks to TestFlight and submissions. Auth uses API keys, and `asc install-skills` adds agent skills.
entries.best_for: Release engineers and agents that automate Apple app shipping in CI or a terminal.
entries.not_for: Only for Apple's App Store Connect, and you need an API key. Releases built with Go 1.27 require macOS 13 or later.

entries.name: Bubble Tea
entries.use_for: Build terminal UIs in Go using the Elm architecture.
entries.why: Standard Go TUI framework (45k stars) with the Charm ecosystem (Bubbles, Lip Gloss).
entries.summary: Bubble Tea is a Go framework for building terminal apps based on The Elm Architecture. It supports inline, full-window or mixed TUIs, with a cell-based renderer, color downsampling, declarative views, keyboard and mouse handling and clipboard support.
entries.best_for: Building interactive terminal user interfaces (TUIs) in Go, simple or complex; pair with Bubbles for common components.
entries.not_for: Go only; assumes familiarity with Go and the Elm-style model/update/view pattern. Not for GUI or web apps.

entries.name: chalk
entries.use_for: Color and style terminal output in Node.js.
entries.why: The most-used terminal styling package (~500M weekly npm downloads).
entries.summary: Chalk is a Node.js library for styling terminal strings with colors and text styles. It exposes a chainable, composable API (e.g. chalk.blue.bgRed.bold) that supports nesting, 256-color and Truecolor, and auto-detects the terminal's color support. It has no dependencies and does not extend String.prototype.
entries.best_for: Adding colors and bold/underline styles to console output in Node.js CLIs and scripts, including custom reusable themes like error or warning styles.
entries.not_for: Layout, tables, prompts or full TUIs; it only styles strings. If bundle size is the top concern, smaller coloring packages exist, though the README argues Chalk is usually already in the dependency tree.

entries.name: Clack
entries.use_for: Build polished interactive CLI prompts and spinners in Node.
entries.why: Modern prompt library (~30M weekly npm downloads) used by create-* scaffolding tools.
entries.summary: Clack provides interactive prompts for JavaScript command-line tools. It ships two packages: @clack/prompts with opinionated, ready-to-use styled prompt components, and @clack/core with headless, unstyled prompt primitives for building your own.
entries.best_for: Node.js CLIs (setup wizards, create-* scaffolders) that need good-looking interactive prompts out of the box, or a headless base to build custom prompt styles.
entries.not_for: Argument and flag parsing or full-screen terminal UIs; it covers interactive prompts only. JavaScript/Node only. The repo README is minimal, so details live in the external docs.

entries.name: clap
entries.use_for: Parse command-line arguments in Rust with derive macros or a builder.
entries.why: The de facto Rust argument parser; rich help, completions and validation.
entries.summary: clap is a command-line argument parser for Rust. You define a parser either declaratively (derive) or procedurally (builder API), and it handles parsing plus the usual features like help output. It is installed with cargo add clap and dual-licensed Apache 2.0 or MIT.
entries.best_for: Rust CLI programs that need argument, flag and subcommand parsing, with a choice between derive-style declarations and a builder API.
entries.not_for: Interactive prompts or terminal UIs; it only parses command-line arguments. Rust only.

entries.name: CLI Printing Press
entries.use_for: Generate an agent-friendly Go CLI, Claude Code skill and MCP server for any API or website.
entries.why: Generated CLIs include a local SQLite store with sync, full-text search and cross-resource commands.
entries.summary: A generator that reads official API docs, existing community CLIs and MCP servers, and can sniff unpublished web APIs. It prints a token-efficient Go CLI with domain SQLite tables, FTS5 search, incremental sync, auto-JSON output when piped, plus a Claude Code skill and MCP server.
entries.best_for: Building a fast offline-capable CLI for an API that agents will use heavily.
entries.not_for: Output quality depends on the source API. Sniffing unpublished web APIs may break a site's terms.

entries.name: Click
entries.use_for: Build composable Python command-line interfaces with decorators.
entries.why: Pallets' CLI library (~18k stars) that Typer and Flask build on.
entries.summary: Click is a Python package for building command-line interfaces by decorating functions with @click.command and @click.option. It supports arbitrary nesting of commands, generates help pages automatically, can prompt for missing values, and supports lazy loading of subcommands at runtime.
entries.best_for: Python CLIs of any size, especially multi-level command groups, where decorator-based declarations with sensible defaults are preferred.
entries.not_for: Projects that want parameters inferred from type hints (Typer, built on Click, does that) or full-screen terminal UIs. Python only.

entries.name: Cobra
entries.use_for: Build Go CLIs with subcommands, flags and generated help and completion.
entries.why: Powers kubectl, Hugo and the GitHub CLI (~45k stars); the Go CLI standard.
entries.summary: Cobra is a Go library for building subcommand-based CLI applications structured as commands, arguments and flags. It provides POSIX-compliant flags, nested subcommands, cascading flags, typo suggestions, automatic help, shell autocomplete and man page generation, plus a cobra-cli generator to scaffold apps. It optionally integrates with viper for configuration.
entries.best_for: Go CLIs with git-style subcommands (app server, app fetch) that need generated help, shell completion and man pages; used by Kubernetes, Hugo and GitHub CLI.
entries.not_for: Interactive prompts or terminal UIs; it is a command/flag framework only. Go only. Possibly heavier than needed for a single-command tool.

entries.name: Commander.js
entries.use_for: Parse arguments and define commands for Node.js CLIs.
entries.why: The most used Node.js CLI framework; tiny, stable API with subcommands and help generation.
entries.summary: Commander.js is a Node.js library for building command-line interfaces. You describe options, arguments and subcommands in code; Commander parses them, reports usage errors (with suggestions for unknown options) and provides an automated, customizable help system. It supports action handlers, stand-alone executable subcommands, lifecycle hooks and TypeScript.
entries.best_for: Node.js CLIs that need option and subcommand parsing with built-in help, from a single script to multi-command tools.
entries.not_for: Interactive prompts or terminal UIs. It is strict by default and errors on unrecognised options, which may not suit permissive parsing needs. Node.js only.

entries.name: Coreutils for Windows
entries.use_for: Use Unix-style commands like ls, grep and find natively on Windows with the same flags as Linux.
entries.why: A Microsoft-maintained single binary of uutils coreutils, findutils and grep.
entries.summary: A packaged multi-call binary of uutils/coreutils, findutils and grep for Windows. The aim is that the same commands, flags and pipelines work as on Linux, macOS and WSL, so scripts carry over.
entries.best_for: Windows users and CI that want familiar Unix tools without WSL.
entries.not_for: Full POSIX behaviour: no signals, no /dev/null, CRLF quirks, and PowerShell aliases can break piped binary streams. It is in preview.

entries.name: DingTalk Workspace CLI (dws)
entries.use_for: Use DingTalk contacts, calendar, docs and more from the command line or from an AI agent.
entries.why: Official DingTalk CLI with JSON output, built-in agent skills and admin-controlled access.
entries.summary: A cross-platform CLI from DingTalk that exposes its product features as commands, such as contacts, calendar, docs, whiteboards and meeting minutes. It uses OAuth device flow, supports dry runs and several output formats, and ships agent skills.
entries.best_for: Scripting or letting agents work with DingTalk enterprise data.
entries.not_for: Needs a DingTalk organization with admin-approved CLI access. Only useful for DingTalk.

entries.name: FTXUI
entries.use_for: Build functional terminal UIs in C++
entries.why: Leading C++ TUI library with a React-like component model and no dependencies.
entries.summary: FTXUI is a cross-platform C++ library for terminal user interfaces in a functional, React-inspired style. It is split into screen (low-level rendering), dom (layout and composition) and component (widgets, events, main loop) modules, with keyboard and mouse navigation, UTF-8 and fullwidth character support, animations and drawing. It has no dependencies.
entries.best_for: C++ applications needing an interactive terminal UI or rich terminal output, packaged via CMake, Bazel, vcpkg, Conan or a single-header amalgamation.
entries.not_for: Non-C++ projects. Linux/macOS are the main target; Windows support is contributor-maintained. Not a command-line argument parser.

entries.name: gitlogue
entries.use_for: Replay git commits in the terminal as an animated typing session.
entries.why: Turns real commit history into a syntax-highlighted replay, useful for demos and screen recordings.
entries.summary: A terminal tool that replays git commits as animation with typing, cursor movement, file tree changes and tree-sitter syntax highlighting for 32 languages. It can show a working-tree diff, replay a commit range, and run in screensaver mode. It has 9 built-in themes.
entries.best_for: Making demos, presentations, teaching material or a decorative terminal from a real git history.
entries.not_for: A visual toy, not a git workflow tool. It is not a real screensaver and may burn in OLED screens.

entries.name: gog (gogcli)
entries.use_for: Script Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs and Sheets from the terminal with JSON output.
entries.why: Offers a read-only mode, explicit account routing and least-privilege Gmail scopes.
entries.summary: A Go command-line client for Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets and more of Google Workspace. Built for people, scripts, CI and agents, it provides machine-readable output, account routing and safety controls. You create your own Desktop OAuth client.
entries.best_for: Automation or agent tools that need safe, scriptable access to Google Workspace data.
entries.not_for: You must set up a Google Cloud project and OAuth client yourself. Not a library for embedding in an app.

entries.name: hunk
entries.use_for: Review code changes in a terminal diff viewer with sidebar navigation and inline agent notes.
entries.why: A review-first interactive UI, unlike pager-style diff tools such as delta.
entries.summary: An interactive terminal diff viewer built on OpenTUI and Pierre diffs. It shows a multi-file review stream with a sidebar, split or unified layouts, watch mode, and mouse and keyboard control. It works as a Git difftool or pager and shows AI annotations inline.
entries.best_for: Reviewing agent-written changes in the terminal.
entries.not_for: Plain diff coloring in pipelines; use delta or difftastic for that. It is meant for interactive review.

entries.name: Ink
entries.use_for: Build interactive terminal UIs with React components.
entries.why: Powers the CLIs of Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Gatsby and more; React model in the terminal.
entries.summary: Ink is a React renderer for command-line apps: you build CLI output from React components, and Yoga provides Flexbox layout in the terminal. All React features are supported, and create-ink-app scaffolds JavaScript or TypeScript projects.
entries.best_for: Node.js developers who already know React and want component-based, stateful, interactive terminal UIs with Flexbox layout.
entries.not_for: Non-JavaScript stacks or minimal CLIs; it requires React and a JSX/Babel or similar transpile setup. Not an argument parser.

entries.name: Inquirer.js
entries.use_for: Ask interactive questions (lists, confirms, inputs) in Node CLIs.
entries.why: The classic Node prompt library (~22k stars), now modular via @inquirer/prompts.
entries.summary: Inquirer.js is a collection of common interactive command-line prompts for Node.js, published as @inquirer/prompts. Each prompt is an async function taking a prompt config and optional context (custom input/output streams, clearing on done, AbortSignal). It was rewritten from scratch for smaller size and better performance.
entries.best_for: Node.js (also Bun and Deno) CLIs that need standard interactive questions such as text input, confirm or select, with async/await usage.
entries.not_for: Argument parsing or full-screen TUIs. Many community prompts from the legacy package may not exist in the new API; the old package is maintained but not actively developed.

entries.name: lark-cli
entries.use_for: Control Lark/Feishu messages, docs, calendar, mail, sheets and more from the terminal or an AI agent.
entries.why: Official CLI with 200+ commands and ready-made agent skills.
entries.summary: The official Lark/Feishu CLI from the larksuite team. It covers messaging, docs, drive, base, sheets, calendar, mail, tasks and meetings. It has a three-layer design of shortcuts, API commands and raw API, and stores credentials in the OS keychain.
entries.best_for: Automating Lark/Feishu work or giving an agent safe access to it.
entries.not_for: Anyone not on Lark or Feishu. It only talks to that platform.

entries.name: Lip Gloss
entries.use_for: Style and lay out terminal output in Go with CSS-like definitions.
entries.why: Companion styling library to Bubble Tea; used across most modern Go CLIs.
entries.summary: Lip Gloss is a Go library of style definitions for terminal layouts, using a declarative, CSS-like API for bold, colors, padding, width and similar properties. It can choose colors at runtime based on the user's terminal and environment. It is designed as a companion to Bubble Tea for building TUI views.
entries.best_for: Go TUIs and CLIs, especially Bubble Tea apps, that need styled boxes, colors and layout without handling low-level terminal details.
entries.not_for: Event handling or app state; it only styles and lays out output and does not replace Bubble Tea. Go only. v2 changes require migration from v1.

entries.name: mgrep
entries.use_for: Search code, PDFs and images by meaning from the terminal.
entries.why: Grep-like feel with natural-language queries and a watch mode that keeps the index fresh.
entries.summary: A CLI that indexes a repo into a Mixedbread store and answers natural-language queries over code, text, PDFs and images. It respects .gitignore, supports web search, and integrates with coding agents to cut token use.
entries.best_for: Finding code by description in large repos, and giving agents better search than grep.
entries.not_for: Needs a Mixedbread account or API key, so indexed content goes to their service. Audio and video are not yet supported.

entries.name: NetWatch
entries.use_for: Watch live network traffic, connections and latency from the terminal and get diagnostic findings against a learned baseline.
entries.why: One binary with no config shows connections, packets with L7 decode, and a rule-based diagnostic engine.
entries.summary: A terminal network diagnostics tool with ten tabs: dashboard, connections, interfaces, packet capture with TLS decryption and JA4, stats, topology and more. It has full, lite (80x24) and dense views, and opens issues when a baseline breaks.
entries.best_for: Sysadmins and developers who want Wireshark-like visibility over SSH or in a tmux pane.
entries.not_for: Deep offline packet forensics at scale. Capture needs sudo or Linux capabilities, and platform support varies.

entries.name: oclif
entries.use_for: Build large, plugin-based CLIs in TypeScript.
entries.why: Salesforce's CLI framework used by the Heroku and Salesforce CLIs; plugins and generators.
entries.summary: This is the oclif CLI for the Open CLI Framework, used to generate and develop oclif-based CLIs and plugins in Node.js. Running oclif generate scaffolds a new CLI from the hello-world example, and generate:command / generate:hook add pieces. Salesforce CLI and Heroku CLI are listed examples.
entries.best_for: Teams building larger, plugin-extensible Node.js/TypeScript CLIs who want scaffolding and framework conventions.
entries.not_for: Small single scripts where a lightweight parser suffices. Requires Node 18+ (LTS versions). This repo is the generator CLI; the framework docs live elsewhere.

entries.name: OfficeCLI
entries.use_for: Let AI agents or scripts read, edit and render Word, Excel and PowerPoint files without Office installed.
entries.why: Single binary with JSON output, stable element paths and HTML or PNG rendering so agents can check results.
entries.summary: OfficeCLI is a command-line tool for creating and editing .docx, .xlsx and .pptx files. Every command can return JSON, elements have stable paths like /slide[1]/shape[2], and a built-in engine renders documents to HTML or PNG so agents can look and fix.
entries.best_for: Agent pipelines or CI jobs that generate reports and slide decks, replacing multi-library Python scripts.
entries.not_for: Rendering is an approximation of Office, not the real thing. Not for editing documents interactively as a person.

entries.name: OpenTUI
entries.use_for: Build performant terminal UIs in TypeScript with React or Solid bindings.
entries.why: Native Zig core with TS bindings; powers the opencode TUI.
entries.summary: OpenTUI is a library for terminal user interfaces with a native core written in Zig and TypeScript bindings, usable directly or through React and Solid renderers. It lays out boxes and text with flexbox and offers selects, inputs and scroll boxes with keyboard and mouse controls, plus sound, images and 3D graphics. Extra packages cover keymaps, QR codes, Three.js and SSH serving.
entries.best_for: TypeScript developers building rich terminal apps with React or Solid; OpenCode uses it in production.
entries.not_for: Non-TypeScript stacks or simple CLIs that only need argument parsing or prompts. Relies on a native Zig core rather than pure JavaScript.

entries.name: Oracle
entries.use_for: Bundle a prompt with chosen files and ask another AI model for a grounded second opinion.
entries.why: Works through an API or a signed-in browser, and shows exactly what it will send before it sends it.
entries.summary: Oracle is a CLI and MCP server that packs a prompt with selected files, sends the context to an AI model via API or a signed-in browser session, and stores the result as a session. A render mode prints the exact bundle without calling any model, and dry-run reports files and token estimates.
entries.best_for: You or your coding agent want a second model to review a real project, with control over which files go in.
entries.not_for: You still need a provider key or a signed-in browser session. Browser mode depends on Chrome and a ChatGPT or Gemini login. Not an agent framework.

entries.name: Pebrel
entries.use_for: Use or fork a GPU-accelerated terminal with split panes, SSH/SFTP and workflows for Claude Code and Codex sessions.
entries.why: Rust and GPUI native app that combines terminals, SSH hosts, file browsing and AI session restore.
entries.summary: A desktop terminal workspace for Windows, macOS and Linux. It has tabs and splits, saved layouts, its own completion engine, an SSH host library with SFTP, Git actions and tracking of AI CLI conversations. It was formerly called Nebula.
entries.best_for: Windows users who live in terminals and AI coding CLIs and want an integrated SSH and sessions workspace.
entries.not_for: Reusing as a library, or embedding in closed-source products: it is a GPL-3.0 desktop application.

entries.name: picocli
entries.use_for: Build CLIs in Java or Kotlin with annotations, help and completion.
entries.why: Most capable JVM CLI framework; supports GraalVM native images.
entries.summary: picocli is a Java library for command-line parsing where you annotate fields with option and parameter names. Implementing Runnable or Callable lets CommandLine.execute parse arguments, handle errors, print usage and version help, and run your logic in one line. Usage help can be customized with ANSI colors via annotations or a Help API.
entries.best_for: Java (JVM) command-line applications that want annotation-based option parsing with colored usage help and built-in error handling.
entries.not_for: Non-JVM projects or full terminal UIs; it is an argument parser and help generator.

entries.name: psmux
entries.use_for: Use tmux-style split panes and sessions natively on Windows.
entries.why: Reads your .tmux.conf and supports tmux commands and themes without WSL.
entries.summary: A terminal multiplexer written in Rust for Windows. It uses ConPTY and speaks the tmux command language, with 90+ commands, split panes, windows, session persistence and mouse support. It installs as psmux, pmux and tmux.
entries.best_for: Windows users in PowerShell or cmd who want tmux workflows without WSL or Cygwin.
entries.not_for: Windows only. Not a full drop-in for every tmux feature, so check the compatibility doc.

entries.name: Ratatui
entries.use_for: Build terminal user interfaces in Rust with widgets and layouts.
entries.why: The standard Rust TUI library (successor to tui-rs), used by many popular Rust tools.
entries.summary: Ratatui is a Rust crate for building terminal user interfaces such as command-line apps, dashboards and interactive console programs. You draw frames using widgets on a terminal backend (e.g. crossterm), and cargo-generate templates provide a quick start.
entries.best_for: Rust developers building interactive TUIs or terminal dashboards who want a flexible widget library with many examples and templates.
entries.not_for: Non-Rust projects or simple CLIs that only need argument parsing. The README lists Cursive and iocraft as alternatives for ncurses-based or declarative styles.

entries.name: Ratty
entries.use_for: Use or study a GPU-rendered terminal emulator that can show inline 3D objects and a 3D mode.
entries.why: A terminal emulator in Rust with inline 3D graphics and a customizable 3D cursor.
entries.summary: A GPU-rendered terminal emulator built with Rust and Ratatui. It supports normal 2D use, a 3D mode, inline 3D objects in .obj, .glb and .stl, a custom cursor model and the Kitty graphics protocol for images.
entries.best_for: Experimenting with 3D in the terminal, or reading how a Rust terminal emulator is built.
entries.not_for: A novelty-leaning terminal emulator, not a library for building your own terminal UI. Building from source needs system packages on Linux.

entries.name: Rich
entries.use_for: Print colored text, tables, progress bars, tracebacks and Markdown in the terminal.
entries.why: Ubiquitous Python terminal formatting library (58k stars); MIT confirmed.
entries.summary: Rich is a Python library for rich text and formatting in the terminal. It adds color and style to output and renders tables, progress bars, markdown, syntax-highlighted code, tracebacks and more through a drop-in print or a Console object. It works on Linux, macOS, Windows and in Jupyter notebooks.
entries.best_for: Python scripts and CLIs that want readable, styled output: pretty tables, progress bars, logging, tracebacks and pretty-printed data.
entries.not_for: Interactive full-screen apps (Textual, from the same team, covers that) or argument parsing. Requires Python 3.8+; classic Windows terminals are limited to 16 colors.

entries.name: Summarize
entries.use_for: Summarize web pages, files, YouTube videos and podcasts from the terminal or a browser side panel.
entries.why: One tool extracts clean text from many sources, with transcript fallbacks and an optional Chrome and Firefox panel.
entries.summary: A Node.js CLI plus Chrome Side Panel and Firefox Sidebar extension. It extracts readable content from pages, PDFs and media, uses published transcripts first, and can call configured models or coding CLIs.
entries.best_for: Quick link-to-summary workflows, or content extraction with JSON output for automation.
entries.not_for: Offline summaries without a model: extraction works with no key, but a model summary needs a provider, local model or authenticated CLI.

entries.name: Terminal.Gui
entries.use_for: Build cross-platform terminal UIs in .NET.
entries.why: The leading .NET TUI toolkit, with a rich widget set.
entries.summary: Terminal.Gui is a cross-platform .NET toolkit for building terminal UI applications on Windows, macOS and Linux. It provides a layout system, double-buffered rendering, keyboard and mouse support, and built-in views like text editors, buttons, trees, tables, menus and markdown. dotnet new templates scaffold new apps.
entries.best_for: C#/.NET developers building sophisticated console applications with windows, forms, tables and menus.
entries.not_for: Non-.NET stacks or simple CLIs that only need output styling or argument parsing. v1 to v2 is a breaking migration.

entries.name: Textual
entries.use_for: Build full terminal (and web) applications in Python with widgets and CSS styling.
entries.why: The most capable Python TUI framework, from the Rich team.
entries.summary: Textual is a Python framework for building user interfaces that run in the terminal or a web browser. It provides widgets (buttons, trees, data tables, inputs, text areas), a flexible layout system, themes, a fuzzy command palette and a testing framework. It is async under the hood but does not force async on you, and textual serve publishes apps to the web.
entries.best_for: Python developers building interactive TUI apps or dashboards that may also need to be served in a browser.
entries.not_for: Simple styled output (Rich is lighter) or plain argument parsing. Python only.

entries.name: tgrep
entries.use_for: Search large codebases with regex much faster than plain grep by using a trigram index and an optional server.
entries.why: Built into GitHub Copilot CLI to speed up grep across large repositories.
entries.summary: A grep that builds a trigram index of your repo. Run tgrep serve to keep the index fresh, or tgrep index for an on-disk index. Searches use the server, then the local index, then fall back to a filesystem scan. Regex literals become trigram lookups.
entries.best_for: Big monorepos where ripgrep or grep gets slow, and agents that run many searches.
entries.not_for: Small repos where grep is already instant. The index can lag changes, and .tgrep/ is build output that must not be committed.

entries.name: Tokscale
entries.use_for: Track token usage and cost across many AI coding agents from your terminal.
entries.why: Reads local data from OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI and more in one dashboard.
entries.summary: Tokscale is a CLI and visualization dashboard that reads local session data from many coding agents to show token consumption and costs. It has views by model, day, hour and session. A submit command can upload stats to an optional leaderboard.
entries.best_for: Developers using several coding agents who want one view of tokens and spend.
entries.not_for: The leaderboard submit feature shares stats publicly, so use only if you want that. Depends on each agent's local file format.

entries.name: tuicr
entries.use_for: Review diffs in the terminal with vim keys and push inline reviews to GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps or Gerrit.
entries.why: One TUI works across git, jj and mercurial and can submit a real review to six code hosts.
entries.summary: A GitHub-style continuous diff in the terminal. You comment on lines, ranges or files, track review progress per file or hunk across sessions, and then export as a hosted review, markdown on the clipboard, or stdout.
entries.best_for: Reviewing your own or agent-written changes before committing, or doing PR reviews without leaving the terminal.
entries.not_for: Browser-based review with rich discussion threads. It is keyboard-driven and terminal only.

entries.name: TUIOS
entries.use_for: Run a terminal window manager with tiled panes, persistent sessions and an inbox for coding agents.
entries.why: A tmux-style multiplexer that also tracks what each coding agent is doing.
entries.summary: TUIOS is a terminal multiplexer built with Go and the Charm stack. It has vim-like modal control, BSP tiling, workspaces, kitty graphics, and a daemon that keeps sessions alive and lets agents report state.
entries.best_for: Developers who run several coding agents in terminal panes and want one view of what each needs.
entries.not_for: Replacing tmux in existing setups without learning its modal keys. Check the docs for the daemon and session model.

entries.name: Typer
entries.use_for: Build Python CLIs from functions using type hints.
entries.why: From the FastAPI author; minimal code, automatic help and completion, built on Click.
entries.summary: Typer is a Python library for building CLI applications from functions using Python type hints, with automatic help and shell completion. It scales from a single typer.run call to trees of commands and subcommand groups. It also includes a typer command that runs scripts as CLIs even if they don't use Typer.
entries.best_for: Python CLIs where you want parameters, help and completion derived from type-hinted function signatures with minimal code.
entries.not_for: Interactive full-screen TUIs. Python only, and it relies on type hints for declarations.

entries.name: urfave/cli
entries.use_for: Build simple, declarative command-line apps in Go.
entries.why: Popular lightweight Go CLI package (~24k stars), alternative to Cobra.
entries.summary: urfave/cli is a declarative Go package for building command-line tools with commands and subcommands (alias and prefix match), a flexible help system and dynamic shell completion for bash, zsh, fish and powershell. Flags support simple types, slices, time and duration, and can be read from environment variables or files. It depends only on the Go standard library.
entries.best_for: Go CLI tools that want declarative command definitions, shell completion and flag values from env vars or config files, with no third-party dependencies.
entries.not_for: Interactive prompts or TUIs. Go only. Man/Markdown docs and structured config file input need separate modules (cli-docs, cli-altsrc).

entries.name: wecom-cli
entries.use_for: Operate WeCom (Enterprise WeChat) messages, mail, docs, todos, calendar, meetings and contacts from the terminal or an AI agent.
entries.why: An official CLI from the WeCom team with an agent skill, covering most WeCom office features.
entries.summary: A command-line tool for the WeCom open platform. It can send bot messages, manage mail, documents, spreadsheets, todos, calendars, meetings and drive files, and read contacts. It is installed with npm and has an agent skill.
entries.best_for: Automating WeCom office tasks, or letting an agent act in a WeCom workspace.
entries.not_for: Needs a WeCom account, and optionally a bot ID and secret. Docs are in Chinese. Useful only if you work with WeCom.

entries.name: whichllm
entries.use_for: Find which local LLM runs best on your GPU, CPU and RAM.
entries.why: Ranks by merged real benchmarks with recency weighting, not just parameter count.
entries.summary: A CLI that auto-detects your hardware and ranks HuggingFace models that fit, using benchmarks such as LiveBench, Aider and Chatbot Arena. It shows memory, estimated speed and fit type, and can simulate a GPU.
entries.best_for: Choosing a local model before you download, or checking what a GPU purchase would let you run.
entries.not_for: Running models. It only recommends; speeds are estimates and depend on live HuggingFace and benchmark data.

entries.name: witr
entries.use_for: Find out why a process, port, container or file lock exists and what started it.
entries.why: Builds a cause chain back to the starter, with JSON output and a TUI.
entries.summary: witr treats every question as a process question: it maps ports, services and containers to a PID, then shows what started it and what keeps it running. It has short output, JSON, exit codes for scripts, and a TUI with process, port, container and lock tabs.
entries.best_for: Debugging a mystery port, service or container on a dev machine or server.
entries.not_for: Full system monitoring or metrics; it explains single processes. Some owners need sudo to show.

entries.name: wterm
entries.use_for: Embed a terminal emulator in a web page that renders to the DOM, so text selection, find and accessibility just work.
entries.why: A Zig core compiled to a small WASM binary, with an optional libghostty backend for full VT compliance.
entries.summary: wterm is a web terminal emulator. The VT100/xterm parser is written in Zig and compiled to a roughly 26 KB WASM file. It draws real DOM rows, which keeps native selection, copy, browser find and screen readers working. React, Next.js and Svelte examples are included.
entries.best_for: Web apps that need an accessible in-browser terminal, such as cloud IDEs, sandboxes and docs demos.
entries.not_for: A canvas-rendered terminal for very heavy output, or a full shell by itself: you still wire up a backend or in-browser shell.

entries.name: yargs
entries.use_for: Parse command-line arguments and build subcommands in Node.js.
entries.why: Hugely used Node argument parser (~270M weekly npm downloads) with help and completion.
entries.summary: Yargs is a Node.js library that parses command-line arguments and generates a help interface. It supports commands, grouped options, a dynamically generated help menu and Bash/Zsh completion scripts, and can also run in the browser. Type definitions come via @types/yargs.
entries.best_for: Node.js CLIs that need flexible argument parsing with commands, option groups, generated help and shell completion.
entries.not_for: Interactive prompts or terminal UIs. TypeScript types live in a separate @types package.

entries.name: zerobrew
entries.use_for: Install Homebrew packages faster with a uv-style client for macOS and Linux.
entries.why: Claims up to 5x faster installs than Homebrew, with an optional brew-compatible command.
entries.summary: A fast client for Homebrew packages that applies uv-style architecture. The `zb` command installs, upgrades and removes packages, and an optional `brew` alias covers common commands. Search, services, tap and casks are not implemented.
entries.best_for: Developers who want quicker Homebrew formula installs and can live without casks and services.
entries.not_for: Experimental. It lacks cask, search, services and tap support, so keep real Homebrew for those.
